transcription.tex: \text{For large powers such as \((x+3)^{20}\), building Pascal’s triangle becomes impractical. The choose function gives any entry directly.}

\text{Number the top row 0 and the first entry 0. Entry \(k\) in row \(n\) is \(\binom nk\): the top number gives the row, the bottom number gives the entry.}\par\text{ The textbook starts counting at 1; here we count from 0 so the numbers match the binomial coefficient directly.}
\text{The triangle is symmetric:\[\binom41=\binom43.\]Choosing one object is equivalent to choosing the three objects to leave out.}

transcription.tex: \text{Pascal’s rule: each interior entry is the sum of the two above it.\[\binom31+\binom32=3+3=6=\binom42\]\[\binom{n-1}{k-1}+\binom{n-1}k=\binom nk\]}

\text{To choose k objects from n, focus on one particular object. Either include it and choose k−1 from the other n−1, or exclude it and choose k from the other n−1. These cases are disjoint and cover every selection.}

\text{\[\binom n2\left(\frac{12n}{5}\right)^2=\binom n3\left(\frac{12n}{5}\right)^3\]\[15=12n(n-2)\quad\Rightarrow\quad4n^2-8n-5=0\]\[(2n+1)(2n-5)=0\quad\Rightarrow\quad n=-\frac12\text{ or }\frac52\]This extension uses the generalised binomial expansion for non-integer n, developed in Year 2.}

transcription.tex: \text{\textbf{a} Find the first four terms, in ascending powers of \(x\), of the binomial expansion of \((1+qx)^{10}\), where \(q\) is a non-zero constant.}
\text{\textbf{b} Given that in the expansion of \((1+qx)^{10}\) the coefficient of \(x^3\) is 108 times the coefficient of \(x\), work out the value of \(q\).}

\text{Coefficient of \(x^3\) is \(120q^3\). Coefficient of \(x\) is \(10q\).\[\begin{aligned}\text{So }120q^3&=108\times10q\\\Rightarrow120q^3-1080q&=0\\\Rightarrow120q(q^2-9)&=0\\\Rightarrow120q(q+3)(q-3)&=0\\q=0,\ q=-3&\text{ or }q=3\end{aligned}\]But as \(q\) is non-zero, \(q=\pm3\).}

transcription.tex: \text{9. A microchip company models the probability of having no faulty chips on a single production run as:}\par\text{\(P(\text{no fault})=(1-p)^n,\quad p<0.001\),}\par\text{ where p is the probability of a single chip being faulty, and n is the total number of chips produced.}
\text{\textbf{a} State why the model is restricted to small values of p.}
\text{Small p makes truncation after p² useful for fixed n. The exact independent-chip probability (1−p)ⁿ does not itself require p<0.001.}
\text{\textbf{b} Given that \(n=200\), find an approximate expression for \(P(\text{no fault})\) in the form \(a+bp+cp^2\).}
\text{\textbf{c} The company wants a 92% likelihood of having no faulty chips on a production run of 200 chips. Use your answer to part b to suggest a maximum value of p for this to be the case.}

\text{\[19900p^2-200p+0.08=0\]\[p=\frac{200\pm\sqrt{33632}}{39800}\]The roots are approximately 0.00963 and 0.000417. Only the latter satisfies p<0.001, so the approximate maximum is p=0.000417 (3 s.f.).}
